claim: Previous studies reported substantial heterogeneity in transmission of many infectious diseases including SARS-CoV-2.
source: Previous studies reported substantial heterogeneity in transmission of many infectious diseases including SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior literature on transmission heterogeneity in infectious diseases.

claim: The number of contacts is rarely considered in approaches studying transmission heterogeneity.
source: However, those results are difficult to interpret since the number of contacts is rarely considered in such approaches.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations in previous methodological approaches, based on review of existing literature.

claim: The pooled estimate suggests that the 20% most infectious cases have 3.1-fold (95% confidence interval: 2.2- to 4.2-fold) higher infectiousness than average cases.
source: By fitting individual-based household transmission models to these data, accounting for number of contacts and baseline transmission probabilities, the pooled estimate suggests that the 20% most infectious cases have 3.1-fold (95% confidence interval: 2.2- to 4.2-fold) higher infectiousness than average cases, which is consistent with the observed heterogeneity in viral shedding.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical modeling results from the analysis of 17 household transmission studies.

claim: The estimated infectiousness variation is consistent with the observed heterogeneity in viral shedding.
source: By fitting individual-based household transmission models to these data, accounting for number of contacts and baseline transmission probabilities, the pooled estimate suggests that the 20% most infectious cases have 3.1-fold (95% confidence interval: 2.2- to 4.2-fold) higher infectiousness than average cases, which is consistent with the observed heterogeneity in viral shedding.
evidence: This claim compares the modeling results with known patterns of viral shedding from the literature.

claim: The '80/20 rule' (i.e., 20% of cases responsible for 80% transmission) has been observed in emerging infectious disease outbreaks.
source: Such phenomena, illustrated by the '80/20 rule' (i.e., 20% of cases responsible for 80% transmission; Adam et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2021), have been observed in emerging infectious disease outbreaks (Lloyd-Smith et al., 2005), including severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) (Shen et al., 2004), Middle East respiratory syndrome (Cauchemez et al., 2016; Cowling et al., 2015), and most recently the COVID-19 pandemic (Adam et al., 2020; Lau et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2021; Wong and Collins, 2020; Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies documenting the 80/20 rule in various disease outbreaks.

claim: The number of contacts per index cases is often not reported in superspreading event studies.
source: However, the number of contacts per index cases is often not reported in SSE studies, and hence not incorporated in the analyses.
evidence: This is a statement about methodological limitations in existing superspreading event studies based on literature review.

claim: Superspreading event studies usually analyze clusters from different settings, in which the baseline transmission risk and density of exposure could be different.
source: In addition, SSE studies usually analyze clusters from different settings, in which the baseline transmission risk and density of exposure could be different (Thompson, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thompson, 2021, discussing heterogeneity in SSE study settings.

claim: Studies of transmission heterogeneity that focus on superspreading events may suffer from publication bias.
source: Finally, studies of transmission heterogeneity that focus on SSEs described in the literature may suffer from publication bias, with larger clusters having higher probability of being observed and reported (Zhao et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 2021, discussing publication bias in SSE studies.

claim: Households are one of the most important settings for SARS-CoV-2 transmission, with 4- to 10-fold higher transmission risk than other places.
source: Households are one of the most important settings for SARS-CoV-2 transmission, with 4- to 10-fold higher transmission risk than other places (Thompson, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thompson, 2021, providing quantitative comparison of transmission risks.

claim: In a household transmission study, an index case is identified, and their household contacts are followed up for 1–2 weeks, during which there is high transmission potential.
source: In a household transmission study, an index case is identified, and their household contacts are followed up for 1–2 weeks, during which there is high transmission potential (Tsang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim describes the methodology of household transmission studies, supported by a citation.

claim: 17 studies were identified, comprising 13,098 index cases and 31,359 household contacts.
source: In total, we identified 17 studies, comprising 13,098 index cases and 31,359 household contacts (Appendix 1—figure 1, Appendix 1—table 1; Bernardes-Souza et al., 2021; Carazo et al., 2022; Dattner et al., 2021; Han et al., 2022; Hart et al., 2022; Hsu et al., 2021; Hubiche et al., 2021; Koureas et al., 2021; Laxminarayan et al., 2020; Layan et al., 2022; Lyngse et al., 2022; Méndez-Echevarría et al., 2021; Posfay-Barbe et al., 2020; Reukers et al., 2021; Wilkinson et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim reports the data collection results from the systematic review, with specific numbers and citations.

claim: Most studies covered a period from January to November 2020, which was dominated by ancestral strains.
source: Most studies covered a period from January to November 2020, which was dominated by ancestral strains, except for Layan et al. (from December 2020 to April 2021) and Hsu et al. (from January 2020 to February 2021), which covered both ancestral strains and the alpha variant.
evidence: This claim describes the temporal coverage and viral variants in the included studies.

claim: For 12 studies out of 14, models with infectiousness variation perform substantially better (range of ∆DIC: 5.8–268).
source: For 12 studies out of 14, models with infectiousness variation perform substantially better (range of ∆DIC: 5.8–268) (Figure 2, Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by model comparison statistics (DIC) from the analysis, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: From 12 studies, the estimated infectiousness variation (σvar) ranged from 1.03 to 2.83.
source: From these 12 studies, the estimated infectiousness variation (σvar) ranged from 1.03 to 2.83.
evidence: This claim reports the range of parameter estimates from the modeling analysis.

claim: The 20% most infectious cases are 2.4- to 10-fold more infectious than the average case.
source: This suggests that, the 20% most infectious cases are 2.4- to 10-fold more infectious than the average case.
evidence: This claim is derived from the range of infectiousness variation estimates (1.03 to 2.83).

claim: Based on the two largest studies with 6782 and 3727 households, the estimated infectiousness variation is 1.48 (95% credible interval [CrI]: 1.29, 1.7) and 1.41 (95% CrI: 1.19, 1.72).
source: Based on the two largest studies with 6782 and 3727 households (Carazo et al., 2022; Lyngse et al., 2022), the estimated infectiousness variation is 1.48 (95% credible interval [CrI]: 1.29, 1.7) and 1.41 (95% CrI: 1.19, 1.72), suggesting that, among all cases, the 20% most infectious are 3.5-fold (95% CrI: 3.0- to 4.2-fold) and 3.3-fold (95% CrI: 2.7- to 4.3-fold) more infectious than the average case.
evidence: This claim reports specific parameter estimates with credible intervals from the two largest studies.

claim: Among all cases, the 20% most infectious are 3.5-fold (95% CrI: 3.0- to 4.2-fold) and 3.3-fold (95% CrI: 2.7- to 4.3-fold) more infectious than the average case in the two largest studies.
source: Based on the two largest studies with 6782 and 3727 households (Carazo et al., 2022; Lyngse et al., 2022), the estimated infectiousness variation is 1.48 (95% credible interval [CrI]: 1.29, 1.7) and 1.41 (95% CrI: 1.19, 1.72), suggesting that, among all cases, the 20% most infectious are 3.5-fold (95% CrI: 3.0- to 4.2-fold) and 3.3-fold (95% CrI: 2.7- to 4.3-fold) more infectious than the average case.
evidence: This claim is derived from the infectiousness variation parameter estimates through mathematical transformation.

claim: The estimated daily probability of infection from outside the household ranges from 0.0003 to 0.017.
source: The estimated daily probability of infection from outside the household and estimated person-to-person transmission probability within households range from 0.0003 to 0.017, and from 0.06 to 0.51, respectively.
evidence: This claim reports the range of parameter estimates from the modeling analysis.

claim: The estimated person-to-person transmission probability within households ranges from 0.06 to 0.51.
source: The estimated daily probability of infection from outside the household and estimated person-to-person transmission probability within households range from 0.0003 to 0.017, and from 0.06 to 0.51, respectively.
evidence: This claim reports the range of parameter estimates from the modeling analysis.

claim: The estimates of parameters for the relationship between number of contacts and transmission range from 0.43 to 0.92, except for the study by Layan et al., 2022, where it is equal to 0.2.
source: The estimates of parameters for the relationship between number of contacts and transmission (larger value indicates stronger inverse association) range from 0.43 to 0.92, except for the study by Layan et al., 2022, where it is equal to 0.2.
evidence: This claim reports the range of parameter estimates from the modeling analysis.

claim: For all studies, the predicted final size distribution is consistent with the observed data and the model fit is judged adequate.
source: For all studies, the predicted final size distribution is consistent with the observed data and the model fit is judged adequate (Appendix 1—Tables 3–7, Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This claim assesses model adequacy based on comparison of predicted and observed data.

claim: Simulation studies demonstrated that there is no important systematic bias, with 88–100% (depending on the parameter) of the 95% credible intervals covering the simulation value.
source: Simulation studies demonstrated that there is no important systematic bias, with 88–100% (depending on the parameter) of the 95% credible intervals covering the simulation value (Appendix 1—table 8).
evidence: This claim reports results from simulation studies validating the estimation algorithm.

claim: A sensitivity analysis that assumes the individual infectiousness of cases follows a Gamma distribution results in substantially worse fit.
source: We conduct a sensitivity analysis that assumes the individual infectiousness of cases follows a Gamma distribution, but the fit worsens substantially (Appendix 1—table 9).
evidence: This claim reports results from a sensitivity analysis comparing different distributional assumptions.

claim: The pooled estimate of infectiousness variation is 1.33 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.95, 1.70).
source: The pooled estimate of infectiousness variation is 1.33 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.95, 1.70), suggesting that the 20% most infectious cases are 3.1-fold (95% CI: 2.2- to 4.2-fold) more infectious than the average case (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim reports the pooled estimate from meta-analysis of 14 studies, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: 5.9% (95% CI: 1.4%, 11.1%) of cases could be at least 8-fold more infectious than average cases.
source: Based on this fitted distribution, we estimate that 5.9% (95% CI: 1.4%, 11.1%) and 14.9% (95% CI: 7.2%, 20.7%) of cases could be at least 8- and 4-fold more infectious than average cases, respectively.
evidence: This claim is derived from the pooled infectiousness variation estimate through mathematical transformation.

claim: 14.9% (95% CI: 7.2%, 20.7%) of cases could be at least 4-fold more infectious than average cases.
source: Based on this fitted distribution, we estimate that 5.9% (95% CI: 1.4%, 11.1%) and 14.9% (95% CI: 7.2%, 20.7%) of cases could be at least 8- and 4-fold more infectious than average cases, respectively.
evidence: This claim is derived from the pooled infectiousness variation estimate through mathematical transformation.

claim: In meta-regression, infectiousness variation is associated with secondary attack rate (SAR).
source: In meta-regression, we find the infectiousness variation is associated with SAR (Appendix 1—table 11).
evidence: This claim reports results from meta-regression analysis examining factors associated with infectiousness variation.

claim: Doubling SAR is associated with 0.55 (95% CI: 0.21, 0.89) unit decrease in infectiousness variation, with R-squared equal to 67%.
source: We estimate that doubling SAR are associated with 0.55 (95% CI: 0.21, 0.89) unit decrease in infectiousness variation, with R-squared equal to 67% respectively.
evidence: This claim reports quantitative results from meta-regression analysis.

claim: The standard deviation of the distribution of number of secondary cases (σsec) is positively associated with mean and SD of number of contacts.
source: Regarding other statistics, we find that σsec is positively associated with mean and SD of number of contacts.
evidence: This claim reports results from meta-regression analysis examining relationships between study characteristics.

claim: There is no association between study statistics and implementation of lockdown, ascertainment method of index and secondary cases, and the circulating virus of SARS-CoV-2 in the study period.
source: Other than these associations, we find no association between these statistics and implementation of lockdown, ascertainment method of index and secondary cases, and the circulating virus of SARS-CoV-2 in the study period.
evidence: This claim reports null findings from meta-regression analysis.

claim: The estimated infectiousness variations are corrected for the variations caused by number of contacts and transmission risks in different settings.
source: Given that we focused our analysis on households with known number of contacts in studies conducted in the early outbreaks caused by ancestral strains, the estimated infectiousness variations are corrected for the variations caused by number of contacts and transmission risks in different settings, difference in pre-existing immunity among contacts (almost everyone is naïve and unvaccinated), and the difference in transmissibility among variants.
evidence: This claim explains the interpretation of the infectiousness variation estimates based on the study design and modeling approach.

claim: The estimated infectiousness variation measures the variation caused by difference in individuals, which may be contributed by both biological factors and host behaviors.
source: Hence, this estimated infectiousness variation measures the variation caused by difference in individuals, which may be contributed by both biological factors and host behaviors, but not other potential confounding factors mentioned above.
evidence: This claim interprets what the infectiousness variation parameter represents based on the modeling approach.

claim: Multiple contact patterns, particularly by age, could contribute to the variations in infectiousness of cases.
source: Regarding host behaviors, multiple contact patterns, particularly by age, could contribute to the variations in infectiousness of cases.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential mechanisms underlying the observed variation.

claim: Mother-child contacts are usually more intense than father-child contacts.
source: For example, mother-child contacts are usually more intense than father-child contacts, and adult cases are more capable of self-isolation within a household compared with children.
evidence: This claim draws on general knowledge about household contact patterns.

claim: Adult cases are more capable of self-isolation within a household compared with children.
source: For example, mother-child contacts are usually more intense than father-child contacts, and adult cases are more capable of self-isolation within a household compared with children.
evidence: This claim draws on general knowledge about behavioral differences by age.

claim: Contact pattern studies suggested that school-age children and young adults tended to mix with people of the same age.
source: Furthermore, contact pattern studies suggested that school-age children and young adults tended to mix with people of the same age (Mossong et al., 2008; Mousa et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to contact pattern studies.

claim: The duration of contact could vary, which could also contribute to the variations in infectiousness of cases.
source: Also, the duration of contact could vary, which could also contribute to the variations in infectiousness of cases (Toth et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation discussing contact duration.

claim: Previous studies suggest that the relative importance of contact characteristics on transmission may be different among viruses.
source: Previous studies also suggest that the relative importance of contact characteristics on transmission may be different among viruses (De Cao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study comparing transmission characteristics across viruses.

claim: Lockdown and stay-at-home orders may increase the time spending at home.
source: For example, lockdown and stay-at-home orders may increase the time spending at home.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the effects of public health measures.

claim: Mask-wearing when in contact with other household members, using separate bedrooms and bathrooms, avoiding having meals together may reduce the transmission in households.
source: Mask-wearing when in contact with other household members, using separate bedrooms and bathrooms, avoiding having meals together may reduce the transmission in households (Ng et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on household transmission prevention measures.

claim: Social disparity such as occupation may increase or reduce the risk of transmission in households, including the availability of personal protective equipment (PPE), or being healthcare worker.
source: Also, social disparity such as occupation may increase or reduce the risk of transmission in households, including the availability of personal protective equipment (PPE), or being healthcare worker (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation discussing social factors affecting household transmission.

claim: The SAR for index cases with fever is 1.4-fold higher than index cases without fever.
source: For example, the SAR for index cases with fever and cough are 1.4- and 1.3-fold higher than index cases without fever and cough, respectively (Madewell et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation providing quantitative estimates of symptom effects on transmission.

claim: The SAR for index cases with cough is 1.3-fold higher than index cases without cough.
source: For example, the SAR for index cases with fever and cough are 1.4- and 1.3-fold higher than index cases without fever and cough, respectively (Madewell et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation providing quantitative estimates of symptom effects on transmission.

claim: Viral shedding is used as a proxy measure of infectiousness.
source: Viral shedding is used as a proxy measure of infectiousness, and consistently it also has substantial variations, as suggested by 11 systematic reviews (Appendix 1—Tables 12–14).
evidence: This claim states a methodological assumption commonly used in infectious disease research, supported by systematic reviews.

claim: Viral shedding has substantial variations, as suggested by 11 systematic reviews.
source: Viral shedding is used as a proxy measure of infectiousness, and consistently it also has substantial variations, as suggested by 11 systematic reviews (Appendix 1—Tables 12–14).
evidence: This claim is supported by references to 11 systematic reviews documenting variation in viral shedding.

claim: Studies report high variations of temporal viral shedding patterns among individuals.
source: Regarding the magnitude of viral shedding, studies report high variations of temporal viral shedding patterns among individuals (He et al., 2020; Jones et al., 2021; Sun et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies documenting variation in viral shedding patterns.

claim: The duration of viral shedding can be highly heterogeneous, with pooled estimates of mean durations ranging from 11.1 to 30.3 days.
source: In addition, the duration of viral shedding can be highly heterogeneous, with pooled estimates of mean durations ranging from 11.1 to 30.3 days, and almost all reviews reporting high heterogeneity of estimates (Cevik et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021b; Díaz et al., 2022; Fontana et al., 2021; Li et al., 2020b; Okita et al., 2022; Qutub et al., 2022; Rahmani et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to systematic reviews reporting heterogeneity in viral shedding duration.

claim: Almost all reviews report high heterogeneity of estimates of viral shedding duration.
source: In addition, the duration of viral shedding can be highly heterogeneous, with pooled estimates of mean durations ranging from 11.1 to 30.3 days, and almost all reviews reporting high heterogeneity of estimates (Cevik et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2021b; Díaz et al., 2022; Fontana et al., 2021; Li et al., 2020b; Okita et al., 2022; Qutub et al., 2022; Rahmani et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from multiple systematic reviews.

claim: Heterogeneities in viral shedding duration still exist in subgroup analyses by age and severity.
source: Such heterogeneities still exist in subgroup analyses by age and severity (Cevik et al., 2021; Fontana et al., 2021; Okita et al., 2022; Qutub et al., 2022; Rahmani et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2020; Yan et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies that performed subgroup analyses.

claim: The infectious period, proxied by duration of replicant competent virus isolation, is heterogeneous.
source: The infectious period, proxied by duration of replicant competent virus isolation, is also heterogeneous (Rahmani et al., 2022; Appendix 1—table 14).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study documenting heterogeneity in infectious period.

claim: One review suggests that heterogeneity in viral shedding is an intrinsic virological factor facilitating higher dispersion parameter for SARS-CoV-2 if compared with SARS-CoV-1 and pandemic influenza A(H1N1)pdm09.
source: One review also suggests that heterogeneity in viral shedding is an intrinsic virological factor facilitating higher dispersion parameter for SARS-CoV-2 if we compare it with the corresponding patterns in SARS-CoV-1 and pandemic influenza A(H1N1)pdm09 (Chen et al., 2021a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review comparing viral shedding patterns across different pathogens.

claim: The observed variation in individual infectiousness is consistent with past analyses of the dispersion parameter in a negative binomial distribution fitted to number of secondary cases per index case of COVID-19.
source: The observed variation in individual infectiousness is consistent with past analyses of the dispersion parameter in a negative binomial distribution fitted to number of secondary cases per index case of COVID-19 (Sun et al., 2021; Wong et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim compares the current findings with previous analytical approaches, supported by citations.

claim: In previous studies of dispersion parameter, the number of contacts was not considered.
source: However, in these studies, the number of contacts was not considered.
evidence: This claim identifies a limitation in previous studies based on literature review.

claim: The SD of the distribution of number of secondary cases (σsec) is only weakly correlated with infectiousness variation.
source: It should be noted that the SD of the distribution of number of secondary cases (σsec) is only weakly correlated with infectiousness variation.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of relationships between study statistics.

claim: σsec is highly correlated with the mean and SD of the number of contacts.
source: This is because σsec is highly correlated with the mean and SD of the number of contacts, suggesting that it may depend on distribution of number of contacts, and hence may not be comparable among studies.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis of relationships between study statistics.

claim: When SAR is higher, it is expected that more contacts are infected and therefore the observed number of secondary cases is less heterogeneous.
source: When SAR is higher, it is expected that more contacts are infected and therefore the observed number of secondary cases is less heterogeneous (Adam et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim provides a mechanistic explanation for the observed association, supported by a citation.

claim: Using other methods besides PCR may lower the sensitivity of detecting infection, resulting in lower estimates of SAR and hence higher estimates of infectiousness variation.
source: One potential reason is that using other methods may lower the sensitivity of detecting infection, resulting in lower estimates of SAR and hence higher estimates of infectiousness variation.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed association between ascertainment method and infectiousness variation.

claim: The study does not have individual-level data.
source: An important limitation of our study is that we do not have individual-level data.
evidence: This is a statement about the study's data limitations.

claim: The study is unable to determine the impact of demographic factors like age and sex on infectiousness variation.
source: Therefore, we are unable to determine the impact of demographic factors like age and sex on infectiousness variation.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations resulting from lack of individual-level data.

claim: The study cannot disentangle the host behaviors from biological factors.
source: Also, we cannot disentangle the host behaviors from biological factors.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations in interpreting the sources of variation.

claim: Previous analysis suggested no evidence of the impact of age on infectiousness of cases.
source: Previous analysis suggested no evidence of the impact of age on infectiousness of cases (Lau et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous analyses.

claim: The study could not include factors affecting susceptibility to infection.
source: In addition, we could not include factors affecting susceptibility to infection.
evidence: This is a statement about model limitations.

claim: The estimates of infectiousness variation capture heterogeneity in infectiousness due to demographic, host, and biological factors.
source: Our estimates of infectiousness variation should be interpreted in light of these limitations: they capture heterogeneity in infectiousness due to demographic, host, and biological factors.
evidence: This claim interprets what the infectiousness variation estimates represent given the study limitations.

claim: In one study that included susceptibility component in the estimation of individual infectiousness, substantial heterogeneity remained with 20% of cases estimated to contribute to 80% of transmission.
source: However, in one study that included susceptibility component in the estimation of individual infectiousness, substantial heterogeneity remained with 20% of cases estimated to contribute to 80% of transmission (Tsang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study that accounted for susceptibility.

claim: The recruitment methods among studies are different.
source: Second, the recruitment methods among studies are different.
evidence: This is a statement about heterogeneity in study methods.

claim: All index cases are laboratory-confirmed in all studies.
source: This may affect the comparability of the results, although all index cases are laboratory-confirmed in all studies (Tsang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim describes a consistent feature across all included studies.

claim: The study assumed that risks of infection from community for all households are the same.
source: Third, we assumed that risks of infection from community for all households are the same, but there were different factors that may affecting this, including occupations, such as healthcare workers, social economic status that related to assess to PPEs (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about a modeling assumption and its limitations.

claim: Most identified studies were conducted in the period of circulation of ancestral strains.
source: Finally, most of our identified studies were conducted in the period of circulation of ancestral strains, and therefore the identified infectiousness variation may not be directly applicable to other variants.
evidence: This is a statement about the temporal and viral context of the included studies.

claim: The identified infectiousness variation may not be directly applicable to other variants.
source: Finally, most of our identified studies were conducted in the period of circulation of ancestral strains, and therefore the identified infectiousness variation may not be directly applicable to other variants.
evidence: This is a statement about the generalizability of the findings to other viral variants.

claim: There is substantial variation in individual infectiousness, which is important for epidemic management.
source: Result indicates that there is substantial variation in individual infectiousness, which is important for epidemic management.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the study findings.

claim: An index case was defined as the first detected case in a household.
source: An index case was defined as the first detected case in a household, while secondary cases were defined as the identified infected household contacts of the index case.
evidence: This is a methodological definition used in the study.

claim: Secondary cases were defined as the identified infected household contacts of the index case.
source: An index case was defined as the first detected case in a household, while secondary cases were defined as the identified infected household contacts of the index case.
evidence: This is a methodological definition used in the study.

claim: The study conducted a systematic review to collect household studies with at least 30 households.
source: We conducted a systematic review to collect household studies with at least 30 households, reporting the number of secondary cases with number of household contacts for each household for COVID-19, in the form of number of households with X cases among households of size Y.
evidence: This describes the systematic review methodology.

claim: The relative infectiousness of case i compared with case j is exp(δi)/exp(δj).
source: The relative infectiousness of case i compared with case j was exp(δi)/exp(δj).
evidence: This is a mathematical definition derived from the model specification.

claim: The parameter β ranges from 0 to 1, with 0 indicating that the transmission rate was independent of number of household contacts while 1 indicated that the transmission rate was inversely proportional to number of household contacts.
source: It ranged from 0 to 1, with 0 indicating that the transmission rate was independent of number of household contacts while 1 indicated that the transmission rate was inversely proportional to number of household contacts (i.e. dilution effect of the contact time per contact which was lower when the number of household contacts is higher).
evidence: This describes the interpretation of a model parameter.

claim: The infectiousness profile f(·) was generated from the assumed incubation period (mean equal to 5 days) and infectious period (mean equal to 13 days).
source: f(·) was the infectiousness profile since infection generated from the assumed incubation period (mean equal to 5 days) and infectious period (mean equal to 13) (He et al., 2020; Jing et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020a; Appendix 1—table 15).
evidence: This describes model assumptions based on cited literature.

claim: The infection time of all cases was unavailable for all studies.
source: Since the data were extracted from publication, the infection time of all cases was unavailable for all studies.
evidence: This is a statement about data limitations.

claim: Inference was conducted under a Bayesian framework using data augmentation Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm.
source: Therefore, we conducted our inference under a Bayesian framework using data augmentation Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to joint estimate the model parameters, the missing infection time, and augmented variables using metropolis-hasting algorithm.
evidence: This describes the statistical inference methodology.

claim: Model adequacy was assessed by comparing the observed and expected number of infections in households by household size.
source: We assessed the model adequacy by comparing the observed and expected number of infections in households by household size.
evidence: This describes the model validation approach.

claim: Models were compared using deviance information criterion (DIC).
source: We compared the model with or without the random effect for variation of individual infectiousness by using deviance information criterion (DIC) (Spiegelhalter et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the model comparison methodology with citation.

claim: Smaller DIC indicates a better model fit.
source: Smaller DIC indicated a better model fit.
evidence: This is a standard interpretation of the DIC statistic.

claim: DIC difference >5 was considered as substantial improvement.
source: DIC difference >5 was considered as substantial improvement (Spiegelhalter et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a methodological criterion supported by citation.

claim: Random effects meta-analyses were conducted using the inverse variance method and restricted maximum likelihood estimator for heterogeneity.
source: We conducted random effects meta-analyses on identified studies to obtain pooled estimates of individual infectiousness, using the inverse variance method and restricted maximum likelihood estimator for heterogeneity (Hedges and Vevea, 1998; Langan et al., 2019; Thompson and Sharp, 1999; Veroniki et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the meta-analysis methodology with citations.

claim: Cochran Q test and the I2 statistic were used to identify and quantify heterogeneity among included studies.
source: Cochran Q test and the I2 statistic were used to identify and quantify heterogeneity among included studies (Cochran, 1954; Higgins et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes the heterogeneity assessment methodology with citations.

claim: An I2 value more than 75% indicates high heterogeneity.
source: An I2 value more than 75% indicates high heterogeneity (Higgins et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a standard interpretation criterion supported by citation.
